title: A Rulebook for Surprises: Commanding Autonomous Aircraft
gist: A U.S. Air Force Collaborative Combat Aircraft test pilot argues the Air Force lacks doctrine to let operators tell correct-but-surprising agentic behavior from malfunction, and proposes a hardware-agnostic 'agent manual' built on probability-quantified risk and operator bandwidth rather than airframe-specific checklists.

themes.theme: Commanding agents requires a new mental model

insights.claim: The core cultural shift needed for autonomous military aircraft is that operators must stop assuming unexpected machine behavior is a malfunction to fix, and instead judge surprising-but-correct agent behavior on its merits, unlike traditional aircraft where lost-contact behavior follows fixed pre-approved actions.
insights.speaker: Greg Search
insights.so_what: Defense-tech investors should watch for doctrine/training-focused programs (not just autonomy software) as the actual bottleneck to fielding agentic combat systems at scale.
insights.quote: Managing autonomy means accounting for a new phenomenon — machine behavior that is both correct and unexpected.
insights.locator: Historically, aircrews have handled surprises by assuming...

insights.claim: Without new guidance to help operators embrace surprising agent behavior, the Air Force risks turning its multi-billion-dollar Collaborative Combat Aircraft autonomy program into 'just another drone' — i.e., a remotely piloted system with none of autonomy's improvisation value.
insights.speaker: Greg Search
insights.so_what: A warning signal that the value of large autonomy procurement programs depends on doctrine catching up with technology, not just hardware delivery — relevant to assessing program risk for CCA-linked contractors.
insights.quote: Unless the Air Force finds a way to train its personnel to embrace surprise when operating agentic aircraft, the service risks turning a multi-billion- dollar autonomy program into just another drone.

themes.theme: The Collaborative Combat Aircraft program architecture

insights.claim: All Collaborative Combat Aircraft variants share a common autonomy core built on the Government Reference Architecture, which decouples software from vehicle hardware to theoretically let agents integrate across different platforms owned by different U.S. services or allies performing similar missions.
insights.speaker: Greg Search
insights.so_what: A hardware-agnostic, government-owned reference architecture reduces vendor lock-in risk and creates a common software layer that allied programs and integrators could plug into — worth tracking who controls this architecture commercially.
insights.quote: All variants share an autonomy core, using Government Reference Architecture. This decouples the software from the vehicle hardware, theoretically permitting agents to integrate across different platforms

insights.claim: Decisions made now on how the Air Force handles autonomous collaborative platforms will become the default template for the rest of its unmanned portfolio and for allied nations standing up their own programs.
insights.speaker: Greg Search
insights.so_what: Early doctrine decisions in this program are a leading indicator for how allied nations' autonomy procurement and rules-of-engagement frameworks will be shaped.

themes.theme: A framework for classifying agent risk

insights.claim: The author's proposed framework classifies agent risk by how hard a task is for the agent (not for a human), quantifies that risk with probability rather than gut instinct, and treats the operator's available cognitive bandwidth as an input to the risk equation.
insights.speaker: Greg Search
insights.so_what: A reusable risk-scoring model (task difficulty for the machine x operator bandwidth) that could generalize beyond aircraft to any human-supervised autonomous fleet, including commercial drone or robotics fleets.
insights.quote: It should classify risk by how hard a task is for the agent, not for the human, and quantify that risk with probability rather than gut instinct.
insights.locator: The missing piece is a hardware-agnostic “agent manual”...

insights.claim: Human intuition about task difficulty does not transfer to agents: a 20-year F-16 close-air-support pilot might struggle switching to a B-2 stealth mission, but an agent has no such categories — it only produces outputs from inputs, so an agent trained for close air support in a rectangular area may adapt more easily to a strike mission than to close air support in a non-rectangular area.
insights.speaker: Greg Search
insights.so_what: A concrete illustration that risk taxonomies built around human mission categories (CAS, strike) will misclassify actual agent risk — implies training/evaluation data for military AI must be organized around input/output boundary conditions, not mission labels.
insights.quote: An agent trained for close air support in a rectangular geographic area may be able to adapt to the strike mission more easily than it can adapt to close air support in a non-rectangular area.
insights.locator: First, classify agents by how hard their tasks are...

insights.claim: Even an agent with 'ten thousand years of perfect training data' would still err if a bug exists in the latest software update, meaning operators must judge how valid training conditions are for live combat rather than assuming trained reliability transfers, and simulators should be used to build reliability heatmaps by task.
insights.speaker: Greg Search
insights.so_what: Reinforces that software-update/version control and simulation-based reliability testing are as critical as model training itself for safety-certifying military AI — a due-diligence checkpoint for procurement.
insights.quote: an agent with ten thousand years of perfect training data would still make an error if there’s a bug in the latest software update
insights.locator: Second, mathematics may be more useful than intuition.

insights.claim: Operator bandwidth should be a formal input to agent-difficulty scoring: the same pilot might safely command only one drone while manually landing a jet with a joystick, but potentially hundreds while monitoring static-area patrols, so the manual should assign higher agent difficulty to tasks with low command availability relative to command demand.
insights.speaker: Greg Search
insights.so_what: Quantifies the human-machine teaming ratio problem (1:1 to 1:hundreds) that determines how much value autonomy programs can actually deliver in combat — a key scalability metric for drone-swarm business cases.
insights.quote: If I’m landing the jet with a joystick, the answer is one. If I’m managing patrols in static geographic areas, it’s potentially hundreds.
insights.locator: Third, the operator’s bandwidth is part of the agent’s input.

insights.claim: Three tempting alternatives to a new agent manual are each rejected by the author: top-down senior-leader directives (removes warfighter judgment on value), vague 'expect the unexpected' language in aircraft manuals (too unenforceable to be useful), and amending Pentagon Directive 3000.09 (too granular a document for sub-system-level detail).
insights.speaker: Greg Search
insights.so_what: Narrows the design space for military AI governance to a specific gap: mission-centric, cross-platform manuals — useful for identifying what kind of contractor or think-tank work will actually get funded.
insights.locator: Three existing approaches to such guidance are tempting...

insights.claim: In live flight tests of Collaborative Combat Aircraft, when the agent made an inappropriate turn while trying to stay within a defined area, the author (as safety pilot) had to override it to a pre-planned heading to avoid risk of an unanticipated mid-air collision — current test-safety staffing depends on a small cohort of subject matter experts that will not scale to other mission sets.
insights.speaker: Greg Search
insights.so_what: A concrete data point on current real-world reliability limits of agentic flight control, and a scaling bottleneck (expert-dependent safety oversight) that autonomy programs must solve before wide fielding.
insights.quote: When the aircraft made an inappropriate turn, I stepped in and commanded it to a pre-planned heading so that there was less of a chance it would turn in a direction the team didn’t expect and potentially cause a mid-air collision.
